    Calculate Simpson's Dominance Index

    Dominance.Rd

    Calculates Simpson's dominance index (lambda), which measures the probability that two randomly selected individuals belong to the same species.

    Dominance(DF, shape = "w")

    Arguments

    DF

    A data.frame containing species abundance data. The first column should contain station names (if shape = "w") or species names (if shape = "l").

    shape

    Data format specification (default = "w"):

    • "w" - Wide format: stations in rows, species in columns (first column = station names) (default)

    • "l" - Long format: species in rows, stations in columns (first column = species names)

    Value

    A data.frame with two columns:

    • Stations - Station or sample names

    • Dominance - Simpson's dominance index (values range from 0 to 1)

    Details

    Simpson's dominance index (lambda) represents the probability that two individuals randomly selected from a sample will belong to the same species. It is calculated as:

    $$\lambda = \sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i^2$$

    where:

    • S = number of species

    • p_i = proportion of individuals belonging to species i

    Values range from 0 to 1:

    • lambda close to 0: Low dominance, high diversity (many species equally abundant)

    • lambda close to 1: High dominance, low diversity (one species dominates)

    The Simpson diversity index (1 - lambda) can be calculated by subtracting this value from 1.

    References

    Simpson, E.H. (1949). Measurement of diversity. Nature, 163, 688. https://doi.org/10.1038/163688a0

    Magurran, A.E. (2004). Measuring Biological Diversity. Blackwell Publishing.

    Hill, M.O. (1973). Diversity and evenness: a unifying notation and its consequences. Ecology, 54(2), 427-432.

    See also

    Shannon for Shannon diversity index, Pielou for evenness

    Examples

    # Example 1: High dominance (one species dominates)
data_dominated <- data.frame(
  Station = c("St1"),
  Sp1 = 90, Sp2 = 5, Sp3 = 3, Sp4 = 2
)
Dominance(data_dominated, shape = "w")  # High value (close to 1)
#>     Stations Dominance
#> St1      St1    0.8138

# Example 2: Low dominance (species equally abundant)
data_even <- data.frame(
  Station = c("St2"),
  Sp1 = 25, Sp2 = 25, Sp3 = 25, Sp4 = 25
)
Dominance(data_even, shape = "w")  # Low value (0.25)
#>     Stations Dominance
#> St2      St2      0.25

# Example 3: Multiple stations
data_multi <- data.frame(
  Station = c("St1", "St2", "St3"),
  Capitella = c(80, 25, 10),
  Owenia = c(10, 25, 30),
  Nephtys = c(5, 25, 30),
  Lumbrineris = c(5, 25, 30)
)
Dominance(data_multi, shape = "w")
#>     Stations Dominance
#> St1      St1     0.655
#> St2      St2     0.250
#> St3      St3     0.280
